Voat doesn't itself host bandwidth-heavy content. What slows down any site of this nature is database access.

Distributing hosting to many home computers would increase latency. This idea is unworkable for a site of this nature. Even onion routing would be faster in comparison, because that network operates at a lower level than database queries.

I just don't foresee it being implementable in a reasonable time frame considering all that already needs to be done with the site codebase and infrastructure currently - plus the resources needed to pull this off properly. The logistics involved to ensure that the system is stable and secure requires a massive amount of coding and testing, and even then there are so many unknowns to account for: network latency across connections is going to be very unpredictable; downtime and failover handling with respect to session connections and database transactions; Privacy and security for all users; opening up the system to sabotage (if enough people who are determined to cause problems for the site host servers and then collectively pull the plug at once, for example). Surely there are ways to try and tackle these issues but there are always going to be trade-offs involved and, again, I'm not sure it is completely feasible or worth it. Those who would have donated their computers (and bandwidth/electricity) to this concept would be better off just contributing that money to the devs for traditional, centralized cloud hosting IMO.

This isn't to shit on your idea - I think it is a great idea if it could be pulled off, but I think even if Voat were to do it it won't happen for a while (or it would have needed to be started from the ground-up as part of the original requirements).

Hi all! I am planning a vacation to Maine this fall, and want to shoot some of the beautiful landscape available to me there. Mostly I'll be in Acadia National Park, and shooting with a new-to-me wide angle (Nikon 10-24) lens on my D5300. I'll have a 35mm and 55-200mm lenses with me as well.

I've never shot wide angle before, and was hoping for some suggestions. I'm a fairly new photographer - my dad has been shooting for decades, and told me that if I'm not comfortable in manual (i'm not) that I should tripod up, shoot aperture priority and save as RAW+JPEG, and convert when I get home.

All I know about RAW is that, well.. it's RAW. It's the unedited version of the image, and my skills in post are.. non-existent. Does converting the file to JPEG automatically edit the image at all? Or do I need to all of the corrections myself?
New wide angle, converting Raw to JPEG for the first time

My image editing software (Photoshop Elements) included a RAW editor and some of my other software (Photomatix Pro for example) imports RAW. In both cases you make the edits and save as a jpeg.

You don't have to spend money on software though. As I understand it GIMPShop has a RAW plugin or you could download RawTherapee. Both are open source offerings.

Sorry I can't offer any suggestions on the landscape thing, I've tried it and failed dismally at capturing a decent image every time. The only thing that I could offer regarding the ultrawide is to be aware of the distortion that is inherent in the lens.

When you have raw image you can individually manipulate different layers of an image. When you convert it to JPEG you can only manipulate image as a whole. If you would like to learn how to edit you should most definitely shoot exclusively in RAW.

My recommendation for you would be is to learn how to properly use camera first. By that I mean try to get proper exposure, accurate colors and decent framing right out of camera. Once you understand how it all works you can move on to editing.

My favorite editing software is Lightroom because it is simple, fast and powerful tool. I learned how to use lightroom using tutorials I found on slrlounge.com

When it comes to wide angle just be aware of the fact that it exaggerates distances and will make whatever is in the foreground/closest to the camera look a lot bigger.

When it comes to RAW you'll have to do some editing, but don't worry it isn't hard stuff.
